evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Positive pressure layer jamming utilizes an inflatable membrane reacting against a rigid constraint frame to compress uncontained jamming layers, surpassing the 14.7 psi atmospheric pressure limit of conventional vacuum jamming.
The soft robotic gripper achieved approximately a 25-fold stiffness variation when positive layer jamming was activated.
Jamming the finger at 45 psi yielded a 1.85 N/mm higher average stiffness than vacuum-equivalent jamming at 14.7 psi and prevented layer slip across the entire 6 mm deflection range.
Pull-out force increased with jamming pressure until saturating at 35 psi with an average force of 80 N, representing a 1.6-fold increase over 12.5 psi and a 1.16-fold increase over 14.7 psi.
Residual deformation (hysteresis) was inconsistent at lower pressures due to layer stiction but consistently approached near zero at and above 35 psi as layers remained in the pre-slip regime.
At 45 psi, the gripper achieved an average opening time of 0.24 s, an average closing time of 0.29 s, and a tip position repeatability standard deviation of 0.13 mm.

Multi-material additive manufacturing combining PETG and TPU enabled direct print-in-place integration of strain-limiting backbones, rigid constraint frames, and 2 mm internal air channels with minimal post-processing.

experimental_setup: Finger stiffness test setup: a single curved gripper finger mounted to a rigid base was deflected by 6 mm using a force sensor on a linear stage over five cycles across pressures from 0 to 45 psi to record force-displacement and hysteresis.

Pull-out force test setup: a two-finger gripper grasped a cardboard tube connected via cord to a force gauge mounted on a linear stage that traversed away until pull-out, tested five times across pressures up to 45 psi.
Tip position repeatability setup: gripper tip coordinates before and after open/close cycles at 45 psi were measured using a linear stage and force sensor.
Actuation characterization setup: electrically controlled solenoid valves and high-speed/slow-motion video were used to determine opening/closing response times and opening pressure.

Functional grasping demonstration: a two-finger gripper was mounted as an end-effector on a UR5 robotic arm with solenoid valves controlled via the UR5 controller to pick up varied payloads up to 1.7 kg.
future_work: Designing and testing a positive pressure jamming link decoupled from the actuator to isolate and optimize stiffness tuning performance.
Evaluating parametric variations including jamming channel dimensions, number of layers, and layer materials.
Implementing positive layer jamming into standard gripper architectures to overcome the lower closing grip force caused by the inverted spring-actuated design.
Enhancing the robustness of multi-material 3D printing to enable more complex soft robotic geometries.
Characterizing the long-term fatigue life and cycling durability of multi-material 3D-printed soft actuators.
Further investigating and characterizing layer stiction transitions and hysteresis phenomena.
independent_variables: jamming bag pressure (ranging from 0 to 45 psi / 310.3 kPa)
limitations_inferred: Operating at 45 psi requires a constant external compressed air supply and pneumatic valving, which restricts untethered or mobile soft robotic applications.
No predictive analytical or numerical mechanics model was established to correlate membrane pressure, contact traction between layers, and resulting flexural rigidity.
The design was evaluated for only one layer thickness (0.13 mm Mylar) and layer count (12 layers), leaving geometric scaling effects uncharacterized in this paper.
Functional grasping was tested primarily on simple geometries (cylinders, blocks, cups), without evaluating grasping performance on irregular or delicate objects.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Stiffness change measurements are not directly comparable to vacuum layer jamming compliant link studies because testing in the curved grasp position included closing grip force in the baseline stiffness value.
The inverted actuator design relying on a 3.7 N constant force spring produces a relatively low grip force, restricting the gripper to specific payload weights and shapes.

Fused deposition modeling with TPU has inferior cycle life compared to silicone molding (e.g., printed 85A TPU failing around 600 cycles versus silicone enduring up to 10^6 cycles in cited literature).
FDM printing of soft filaments demands specialized hardware, low printing speeds, and careful parameter tuning to achieve airtightness.
Hysteresis was highly inconsistent at lower pressures due to unpredictable stiction between Mylar layers.
Manufacturing and assembly variations introduced minor inter-finger differences, such as differing opening pressures between fingers.
Fatigue life of the multi-material 3D-printed actuators was not fully characterized.
main_results: The positive layer jamming soft gripper demonstrated an approximate 25-fold stiffness variation.
Jamming at 45 psi provided an average stiffness increase of 1.85 N/mm over vacuum-equivalent jamming (14.7 psi) and eliminated slip across a 6 mm deflection range.
Gripper pull-out force reached a plateau at 35 psi with an average of 80 N, yielding a 1.6-fold increase over 12.5 psi and a 1.16-fold increase over 14.7 psi.
Hysteresis consistently dropped near zero at pressures of 35 psi and above as the jamming layers remained locked in the pre-slip regime.
Gripper tip repeatability exhibited a standard deviation of 0.13 mm at 45 psi.
Average actuation times at 45 psi were 0.24 s for opening and 0.29 s for closing.
Full opening of the finger against the internal 3.7 N spring required 45 psi of bellows pressure.
The UR5-mounted dual-finger gripper successfully grasped payloads up to 1.7 kg with layer jamming enabled.
performance_metrics: average bending stiffness increase (1.85 N/mm increase at 45 psi over 14.7 psi)

actuation opening time (0.24 s) and closing time (0.29 s)
full opening actuation pressure (45 psi / 310.3 kPa)

residual deformation / hysteresis (near zero above 35 psi)
possible_gap_implications: Demonstrating that layer jamming can operate under positive pressure rather than sub-atmospheric vacuum shows that jamming force is not fundamentally capped by 1 atmosphere, opening possibilities for significantly higher payload-to-weight soft robotic joints.

The integration of multi-material additive manufacturing demonstrates a viable alternative to labor-intensive silicone casting for pneumatic actuators with embedded rigid jamming constraints, though material fatigue life remains a gap to resolve.

Evaluating stiffness in a pre-curved actuated configuration highlights that actuation pre-loads confound pure variable-stiffness metrics, emphasizing the need for isolated link characterization protocols.
paper.research_objective: Develop, fabricate via multi-material 3D printing, and experimentally evaluate a soft robotic gripper with tunable stiffness enabled by a novel positive pressure layer jamming mechanism that achieves higher stiffness variation and payload capacity than conventional vacuum-based layer jamming.
paper.research_problem: Soft robots possess inherent compliance and safety advantages but are severely limited in payload capacity. Conventional variable stiffness approaches like vacuum layer jamming are constrained by atmospheric pressure (maximum 14.7 psi / 101.4 kPa), while conventional silicone molding for soft actuators requires intensive assembly and cannot readily produce complex airtight multi-material structures.
paper.title: A 3D Printed Soft Robotic Gripper With a Variable Stiffness Enabled by a Novel Positive Pressure Layer Jamming Technology
